 Winter Park may reconsider league’s use of fields in wake of viral youth soccer incident 
 Mayor joined others on dais during meeting to address weekend match where officials called police about 3-year-old player and his parents

 An image from the GoFundMe account created by Martasia Griffin, the mother of Nevada Pierre, earlier this week to “Support Nevada’s Soccer Journey” had raised more $56,000 (with a goal of $30,000) as of Thursday morning. Video of an incident Saturday at a youth soccer match in Winter Park where Nevada was playing has gone viral. (Image from GoFundMe) 
 By Brian Bell | bbell@orlandosentinel.com | Orlando Sentinel PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 2:15 PM EDT | UPDATED: October 29, 2026 at 3:06 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Winter Park officials , upset by a viral incident at a youth soccer match, may reconsider whether the sports league should continue using city fields, with one commissioner criticizing everyone but the children involved in the spat that brought police to the weekend game.
 Commissioner Craig Russell, a longtime teacher and athletic coach at Winter Park High School, said he was disappointed in the conduct of adults in the Saturday morning i9 Sports youth soccer match at Martin Luther King Jr. Park.
 “The true measure of a great youth sports program isn’t how talented any of the kids are, the players are, it’s really how the adults model the respect, sportsmanship and self control and character,” Russell said.
 The city is waiting for i9, which runs a variety of youth sports leagues in Florida and across the country, to conduct its review of the incident, which drew hundreds of thousands of views online and prompted claims of racism.
 Mayor Sheila DeCiccio said “we will look at it once that review is done as to whether we go forward or not with them.”
 A local civil rights group urged the city to investigate.
 A league official called Winter Park police and said Martasia Griffin, the mother of a 3-year-old boy named Nevada, was being disruptive, following him around and calling him names, according to audio of his  911 call.
 He told officers that Nevada was more advanced than the other kids in the league — v ideo shows him easily dribbling the ball around other players and scoring again and again — and that he had previously taken the boy off the field so other kids could play, which prompted criticism from Nevada’s parents.
 Winter Park police on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, were called on the family of a 3-year-old boy during his youth soccer game at Martin Luther King Jr. Park. This image, taken from police body-worn camera footage, shows the boy's parents, Don Pierre and Martasia Griffin, talking to officers as their son, Nevada, stands in the background. (Courtesy Winter Park Police Department) 
 The official also told officers that Nevada sometimes pushes other kids, and had during Saturday’s game, and that when he tried to speak with referees, the boy’s parents started arguing with other parents and caused a “big scene.”
 However, Griffin told police the official has been doing “weird” things to Nevada for weeks because of his talents, insisting she hadn’t cursed at anyone and that Nevada hadn’t hit any of the other children.
 The footage shows officers walked with the family to one of the park’s exits. A news release from the agency stated they weren’t forced to leave the park.
 Nevada and his parents are Black, as is the official who talked to police, according to footage of the incident. But many who watched videos posted by Griffin online accused the league of not wanting Nevada to succeed because of his race.
 Russell said Winter Park has become the scapegoat because the incident took place at its facilities, but those who rent them bear responsibility for what happens at their events.
 “We’re on national news because it happened in our backyard,” Russell said. “We’ll look more deliberately on the leagues that conduct business in here because we have a standard to protect kids, especially, and safety to our residents.”
 He stressed the adults behaved poorly.
 “I hope that that young man — I’m sorry, I hope that baby is OK, that 3-year-old child is OK, I hope that the 5- and 6-year-old babies are OK, and that there’s a resolution that is acceptable in regards to moving forward,” Russell said.
 DeCiccio said police treated the incident as a civil matter between two parties.
 “No one was arrested, no one received a trespass warning, no one was asked to leave,” she said. “The parents told officers the game was over, and they were leaving. Removing a player from the program was the league’s decision, the city had no part in it.”
 However, police body-cam footage from the encounter show an officer did ask the family to leave.
 “One of the coaches advised that they don’t want you guys here anymore, okay? If you guys don’t mind leaving, it would be very much appreciated,” the officer said, according to the video.
 The 911 call, police report and the officers’ body-cam footage are publicly available on the police department’s website.
 Lawanda Thompson, representing Equity Council Corp . of the Orlando area, was the sole person to speak on the issue during public comment and encouraged commisioners to conduct their own formal review of i9 Sports’ continued use of city-owned athletic facilities.
 “This incident has raised serious community concerns about the treatment of young children and families participating in recreation programs, the handling of disputes by private sports organizations and the appropriate involvement of law enforcement,” Thompson said.
 “The circumstances require a fair review and the allegations of discrimination must be evaluated on the evidence,” Thompson said.
 The sports league did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson said Monday that i9 has reached out to Nevada’s family as part of its review.
 Video of the police encounter recorded by Griffin has been shared on her son’s Instagram and TikTok accounts, each with hundreds of thousands of followers, and have been reposted across social media by other accounts.
 A GoFundMe account created by Griffin earlier this week to “Support Nevada’s Soccer Journey” had raised more $59,000 as of Thursday from more than 2,200 donations.
 “What should have been a happy childhood moment became heartbreaking and distressing for him and deeply painful for our family to witness,” Griffin said in her message. “This fundraiser is about more than one painful experience. It is about protecting Nevada’s passion for soccer and making sure this moment does not define his journey.”
 Attempts to reach Griffin through the account, as well as by using a phone number and email address listed in public records, were not successful.
 Eddie Johnson, the former U.S. men's national team player who runs EJE7 Soccer Academy in Orlando, posted Tuesday on his Instagram account an offer to start training Nevada in January. (Image from Instagram) 
 Eddie Johnson, the former U.S. men’s national team player who runs EJE7 Soccer Academy in Orlando, posted Tuesday on his Instagram account an offer to start training Nevada in January.
 “Nevada deserves to be around someone that looks like him, that can understand him and it’s sad in youth soccer we don’t have enough of those programs for kids of color to have those examples around them,” Johnson wrote in his post.
 “We should be praising a three year old with his ability instead of tarnishing it,” Johnson added
 Attempts to reach Johnson for comment through the account were not successful.
